subject: religious-studies
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: How would a virtue ethicist most characteristically approach a question in sexual ethics?
options: By applying an absolute universal law
By identifying the most loving outcome
By asking what a person of good character, exercising the virtues, would do
By calculating the pleasure and pain produced
questions.explain: Virtue ethics focuses on character, asking what action expresses and develops the virtues rather than weighing consequences or applying rules.

questions.q: In Fletcher's personalism, the principle means that ethics:
options: Puts people at the centre rather than rules
questions.explain: Personalism places people, not legalistic rules, at the heart of moral decision-making.

questions.q: In Aristotle's virtue ethics, the distinction between intellectual and moral virtues is that moral virtues are acquired through:
questions.explain: Aristotle holds that moral virtues develop through habituation, whereas intellectual virtues largely come through teaching.

questions.q: G. E. Moore's 'naturalistic fallacy' is the error of:
options: Defining 'good' in terms of any natural property
Deriving an ought from an is
questions.explain: Moore argued that 'good' is a simple, non-natural and indefinable property, so identifying it with any natural property commits the naturalistic fallacy.

questions.q: Act utilitarianism, associated with Bentham, judges the rightness of an action by:
options: Whether it follows a general rule that maximises utility
The consequences of that particular act in producing the greatest happiness
Its conformity to the categorical imperative
questions.explain: Act utilitarianism assesses each individual act directly by how much net happiness it produces.

questions.q: A Kantian objection to a business deceiving customers for profit appeals chiefly to the idea that the firm:
options: Treats customers merely as means to an end
Cultivates a vice rather than a virtue
questions.explain: Deception uses people merely as instruments for profit, violating Kant's formula of humanity that persons be treated as ends.

questions.q: R. M. Hare's prescriptivism argues that moral statements primarily function to:
options: Prescribe or recommend a course of action universally
Merely vent emotion with no guidance
Report intuitions of a non-natural property
questions.explain: Prescriptivism holds that moral judgements are universalisable prescriptions telling people what to do, going beyond mere expressions of feeling.

questions.q: A natural law assessment of contraception traditionally regards it as problematic because it:
options: Frustrates the primary precept of reproduction
questions.explain: Natural Law treats reproduction as a primary precept, so deliberately preventing procreation in the sexual act is seen as contrary to its natural end.

questions.q: For Aristotle, eudaimonia is best translated as:
questions.explain: Eudaimonia is the final end for humans, often rendered as flourishing or living and faring well, achieved through virtuous activity.

questions.q: For Aristotle, phronesis (practical wisdom) is important because it:
options: Enables one to discern the right action in particular situations
questions.explain: Phronesis is the practical reasoning that lets a person identify and choose the mean in concrete circumstances.

questions.q: In meta-ethics, cognitivism is the view that moral statements:
options: Are propositions that can be true or false
Merely express emotions and have no truth value
questions.explain: Cognitivism holds that ethical statements assert facts and are capable of being true or false.

questions.q: In Aquinas's account of conscience, synderesis is:
options: The innate disposition to pursue good and avoid evil
An emotional sense of guilt instilled by parents
The voice of God speaking directly to the soul
The act of applying knowledge to a particular case
questions.explain: Synderesis is the natural inner principle directing us toward good and away from evil, distinct from conscientia, the act of applying it.

questions.q: Mill's distinction between higher and lower pleasures holds that higher pleasures are those of:
options: The intellect, imagination and moral sentiments
questions.explain: Mill ranked intellectual and moral pleasures as qualitatively higher than mere bodily pleasures.

questions.q: Kant's formula of humanity requires that we treat humanity:
options: Never simply as a means, but always also as an end
As a means whenever it maximises utility
Always merely as a means to our ends
Only when it serves the social contract
questions.explain: The humanity formula forbids using persons merely as instruments, demanding they always be respected as ends in themselves.

questions.q: Situation Ethics is best classified as a theory that is:
questions.explain: Situation Ethics is teleological (judging by the loving end) and relativist (rules may be set aside to serve agape).

questions.q: In business ethics, the principle that a company has obligations beyond shareholders to employees, consumers and the wider community is known as:
questions.explain: Corporate social responsibility holds that businesses bear duties toward a range of stakeholders, not just maximising shareholder profit.

questions.q: How might a situationist approach euthanasia?
options: By asking whether ending the person's life is the most loving act in the situation
By forbidding it under an absolute rule against killing
By calculating the total quantity of pleasure and pain
By appealing to the formula of universal law
questions.explain: Situation Ethics judges each case by agape, so euthanasia could be right if it is the most loving response to that situation.

questions.q: Which is one of Fletcher's four working principles in Situation Ethics?
questions.explain: The four working principles are pragmatism, relativism, positivism and personalism.

questions.q: Kant's categorical imperative is categorical because it:
options: Commands unconditionally, regardless of one's desires or goals
Depends on the consequences of an action
questions.explain: A categorical imperative binds absolutely and unconditionally, unlike a hypothetical imperative that depends on a desired end.

questions.q: Hume's 'is-ought' problem points out that arguments often:
options: Treat moral claims as mere commands
Move from descriptive statements to prescriptive conclusions without justification
Define good in terms of a natural property
questions.explain: Hume noted that writers slide from statements of fact (is) to moral claims (ought) without explaining how the transition is warranted.

questions.q: Freud's account of conscience locates it in the:
questions.explain: For Freud, conscience is a function of the super-ego, formed by internalised parental and societal authority rather than reason or God.

questions.q: A natural law approach to voluntary euthanasia would most likely judge it wrong because it:
options: Violates the primary precept of preserving life
Is not the most loving option
questions.explain: Natural Law upholds the preservation of life as a primary precept, so deliberately ending life conflicts with that basic good.

questions.q: Moore's intuitionism claims that the property of goodness is known by:
questions.explain: For Moore, 'good' is non-natural and grasped directly by intuition rather than defined or empirically observed.

questions.q: Aquinas's doctrine of double effect permits an action with a bad side-effect provided that:
options: The agent feels no guilt about the outcome
The good consequences outweigh the bad in a calculation
The bad effect is intended as a means to the good end
The act itself is good or neutral and the bad effect is not intended
questions.explain: Double effect requires that the act be morally good or neutral, the bad effect foreseen but unintended, and the good effect not achieved through the bad.

questions.q: Emotivism is classified as a meta-ethical theory that is:
questions.explain: Emotivism is non-cognitivist because it denies that moral statements state facts or have truth value.

questions.q: The first formulation of Kant's categorical imperative, the formula of universal law, states that one should:
options: Follow the loving thing to do in each situation
Act only on a maxim you could will to become a universal law
Always maximise happiness for the greatest number
Treat the consequences as the measure of duty
questions.explain: The universalisability formula requires acting only on maxims that could consistently be willed as universal laws without contradiction.

questions.q: For Kant, an action has genuine moral worth when it is done:
options: From duty, out of respect for the moral law
questions.explain: Kant holds that only actions performed from duty, for the sake of the moral law itself, have moral worth.

questions.q: Kant calls a good will good because:
options: It is good in itself, without qualification
questions.explain: The good will is the only thing good without qualification; its value lies in willing rightly, not in its effects.

questions.q: Aquinas's conscientia refers to:
options: A faculty that is always infallible
The innate orientation toward the good
Reason making particular moral decisions and applying principles
questions.explain: Conscientia is the activity of reason applying the principles of synderesis to specific situations, and it can err.

questions.q: In Aquinas's Natural Law, the precepts that are universal and self-evident, derived from the rational nature of human purpose, are known as the:
questions.explain: Primary precepts are the unchanging, self-evident goals that flow from human nature, such as preserving life and reproducing.
